title: RESOLVED: provider and conformance implementation are not a trade; mimid is both
description:
Mark, 2026-11-22. The decision that should come BEFORE the hard
blockers are finished, because the two paths diverge sharply after them.

His own framing: '"Plug into all of them" reads as a feature-
completeness problem and isn't.' mimid has interop-tested with ONE
implementation, cooperatively, with its author answering email. The work
is interop testing and it does not compress.

OPTION A: full provider. mimid is a provider people use, federating
with gatekeepers. Needs the whole content list (read receipts, AV
metadata, calls, typing, polls, location, stickers, attachments at
volume), multi-device under load, discovery past a configured peer map,
and a working abuse path across E2EE. This is where mandated interop
VISIBLY fails for users: not refused messages, but messages arriving as
"unsupported content".

OPTION B: the independent conformance implementation. If the EU mandates
MIMI, someone has to be able to CHECK whether the gatekeepers' claims
are true. That is a conformance target, and mimid is already closer to
filling it than any gatekeeper's internal stack: strict decoding, the
fixture-test direction fixed, every ambiguity a decision bead, a
findings log, offline tests. It needs far LESS of the content list,
because a conformance tool has to parse and judge content, not render
it.

What each path makes of the same work:
- The hard blockers are needed either way: catch-up, provider auth,
  ciphersuites, identity. Both paths cross them.
- Content coverage is almost entirely A. A conformance tool needs to
  decode and check content-10, which mimid largely does, not to show a
  sticker.
- Multi-device at volume is mostly A.
- Discovery past the peer map is mostly A. A conformance checker is
  pointed at a target deliberately.
- Franking and reportAbuse are BOTH, and arguably more important to B:
  checking that a gatekeeper's abuse path actually works across E2EE is
  exactly the sort of claim a regulator cannot verify itself.
- The decision-bead discipline and the findings log are B's product.
  Under A they are internal hygiene.

NOT DECIDED. This is Mark's to make, and it is a strategy question, not
a technical one. Recorded so the hard-blocker work is not finished
before it is asked.

Worth noting for either answer: B does not require giving up being a
usable provider, and A does not forbid publishing conformance vectors.
The question is which one sets the priority order when they disagree,
and they disagree about the whole content list.
notes:
CLOSED 2026-11-22 as a FALSE TRADE. Mark: "i honestly dont get why
'both' is so expensive." He was right, and this bead's framing was
wrong twice over.

WHY IT WAS WRONG. The arithmetic I implied was
cost(both) = cost(provider) + cost(conformance). It is not. The
conformance capability is already built and already maintained:

- strict decoding that refuses trailing bytes, non-minimal lengths and
  unknown enum values (AGENTS.md; decision mimid-1wgh.52 item 1);
- the fixture test direction fixed, so a passing test means something;
- a decision bead per ambiguity, with the competing readings;
- the findings log, and offline tests.

And decision mimid-1wgh.52 item 2 already describes the referee act in
production: when a peer trips a stated rule, mimid refuses and "show
them the section; that is how today's Haven fixes happened." mimid has
been acting as a conformance implementation all along, from inside a
provider. There was never a fork to choose.

So the real cost is the content list, and it is the same either way.
Being a referee as well adds no hours to implementing calls or read
receipts. cost(both) = cost(provider) + small.

THE TWO COSTS THAT DO SURVIVE, neither of them engineering hours:

1. Standing. A referee that is also a competitor is not disinterested.
   Thin for mimid: Mark is not a gatekeeper and mimid is not a
   commercial competitor. It would only bite if mimid became a large
   provider, which is not the current trajectory.
2. The accuracy bar, and this is the real one. Publishing findings about
   other implementations raises the cost of being wrong. Evidence from
   this session alone: three "findings" about Haven dissolved on
   checking -- their DNS key record existed (I queried our selector and
   dropped a label), their directory was well formed, their client
   certificate already carried the dNSName SAN. Each was my own bug
   wearing a finding's clothes. In a bead that is a correction; in a
   published conformance report about a gatekeeper under a legal
   mandate it is a retraction. Carried forward as its own bead rather
   than as a strategy fork.

CONSEQUENCE, applied: the dependency that blocked mimid-7yn7.5 (the
content list) behind this decision is REMOVED. It was predicated on the
trade being real. The content list is now ordinary prioritised work,
competing on merit with the hard blockers rather than gated on a
strategy question that turned out not to exist.
